chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Muhammad, from Mu'alla ibn Muhammad, from Al-Hasan ibn Ali, from Aban ibn Uthman, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Abdillah, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a group of people who jointly inherited a slave, and one of them emancipated his share of him. How would the one who emancipated his share be dealt with? Would he be held accountable for what remains? He said: Yes, he would be held accountable for what remains of him, at his price on the day he emancipated (his share).

key_terms.أَعْتَقَ: Emancipated (i'taq) — the legal act of freeing a slave, one of the most meritorious acts in Islamic law
key_terms.بِقِيمَتِهِ: At his price/value — the market value of the slave on the day of emancipation, used as the basis for compensation to co-owners
key_terms.عَبْداً: Male slave (raqiq) — a legally recognized form of ownership in classical Islamic law, addressed extensively in the books of fiqh
key_terms.نَصِيبَهُ: His share/portion — each heir's fractional ownership in the jointly owned slave
key_terms.وَرِثُوا: Jointly inherited — when an estate passes to multiple heirs, shared ownership (shuyua') is created with fractional shares

ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic ruling when one co-owner emancipates his share of a jointly owned slave?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) ruled on the case of a jointly inherited slave where one co-owner emancipates his share. In classical Islamic jurisprudence, such an act by a solvent co-owner triggers an obligation to purchase and free the remaining shares at the slave's market value on the day of emancipation. This ruling reflects the legal principle that partial emancipation should lead to complete freedom, protecting the slave from remaining in a divided state of servitude.
